meta.title: Mobile In-App SDK Market Research
meta.subtitle: Technical capabilities, differentiators and proprietary tech across the mediation, bidding and demand-side SDK landscape.

sdks.name: AppLovin MAX
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Runs a continuous multi-armed-bandit auction (Axon) that feeds both MAX (mediation) and AppDiscovery (AppLovin's own DSP) — a genuine data flywheel and the industry's largest mediation footprint.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Runs its own demand inside the same auction it operates as mediator; has drawn sustained developer criticism and a disputed 2025 short-seller fraud allegation over related-party UA/mediation loops.
sdks.adFormats: Banner (incl. MREC), Interstitial (incl. video), Rewarded video, Native
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid: unified real-time in-app bidding auction across 20+ SDK bidders plus 25+ waterfall networks, run through the Axon engine.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android, Unity, React Native, Flutter, Cocos2d
sdks.reporting: MAX Dashboard, Mediation Debugger, impression-level data, Axon AI yield optimization
sdks.privacy: ATT, GDPR/EU consent APIs, US state privacy APIs; publisher responsible for CMP integration
sdks.positioning: Mid-size to large publishers, especially gaming, with 100K+ DAU; dual-sided platform also serving advertisers via AppDiscovery
sdks.pricing: Free to publishers; monetizes advertiser side. Sources disagree on the exact mechanism/rate — none authoritative, treat as approximate.
sdks.demandNetwork: 20+ SDK bidders and 25+ traditional ad networks in the unified auction
sdks.proprietaryTech: Axon: continuous multi-armed-bandit auction optimization; every impression is a live learning opportunity feeding both MAX and AppDiscovery
sdks.marketShare: >80% mediation market share per mid-2026 sources (vs ~60% in 2024 estimates); FY2025 revenue $5.48B (+70% YoY)
sdks.sources: AppLovin Support Center; Segwise; Playwire; The Register; Naavik

deck.name: AppLovin MAX
deck.blurb: Axon runs a continuous multi-armed-bandit auction feeding both MAX and AppDiscovery. >80% mediation share per mid-2026 sources; FY2025 revenue $5.48B, +70% YoY.
deck.risk: Runs its own demand inside the auction it operates; sustained developer criticism plus a disputed 2025 short-seller fraud allegation.

sdks.name: ironSource / Unity LevelPlay
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Deepest Unity Editor/Cloud integration in the category; demand side is being rebuilt around Vector, a from-scratch neural-network ad engine using engine-level gameplay data no SDK-only competitor can see.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Mid-restructuring: Unity discontinued the standalone ironSource Ads Network effective April 30, 2026, while LevelPlay mediation continues. Same self-preferencing critique as AppLovin/AdMob.
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid: unified auction (bidding) plus waterfall, run natively inside the Unity Editor/dashboard.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android; deepest integration inside Unity Editor/Unity Cloud; usable outside Unity via native SDKs
sdks.reporting: LevelPlay dashboard, A/B testing, real-time monetization data
sdks.privacy: GDPR consent methods, US state privacy, ATT
sdks.positioning: Developers building in/alongside the Unity Editor; gaming-first, deep engine-level integration
sdks.demandNetwork: Unified auction across leading SDK networks and bidders; smaller top-game footprint than AppLovin
sdks.proprietaryTech: Unity Vector: rebuilt neural-network ad engine, successor to 2021's Audience Pinpointer; fuses gameplay, monetization and campaign signals into one self-learning model
sdks.marketShare: Unity FY2025 total company revenue $1.85B; LevelPlay is part of the restructured 'Strategic Grow' segment
sdks.sources: Unity LevelPlay product page; Unity Investor Update Q1 2026; AdExchanger; Mobile Dev Memo; Naavik

deck.name: Unity LevelPlay
deck.blurb: Deepest Unity Editor and Unity Cloud integration in the category. Vector is a from-scratch neural ad engine using engine-level gameplay data no SDK-only rival can see.
deck.risk: Mid-restructuring: the standalone ironSource Ads Network was discontinued 30 April 2026 while LevelPlay mediation continues.

sdks.name: Google AdMob
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Broadest platform support and the lowest barrier to entry; direct pipe into Google's own Search/Display advertiser demand that no independent SDK can access.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Same self-preferencing critique as AppLovin/Unity — Google's own demand competes in the auction it operates. Not shown as the top platform by top-grossing-game share in third-party samples.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, Native, App Open
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid: 'Open Bidding' real-time auction plus waterfall, unified via 'mediation groups'.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android, Unity, Flutter, React Native (Google Mobile Ads SDK plugins for all)
sdks.privacy: Must use a Google-certified CMP for GDPR/UK; US state privacy law support built into SDK setup flow
sdks.positioning: Indie/small developers and anyone already in the Google Ads ecosystem; easiest on-ramp
sdks.pricing: Not officially published; a widely cited 'up to 40%' figure comes from a third-party comparison, not Google.
sdks.demandNetwork: Connects to essentially every major third-party network, backed by Google's own advertiser demand
sdks.proprietaryTech: 'Open Bidding' real-time auction infrastructure; deep integration with Google's broader ads ecosystem
sdks.marketShare: Extremely broad adoption as a baseline/default SDK, especially among smaller publishers
sdks.sources: Google AdMob Help Center; MonetizeMore; Teqblaze

deck.name: Google AdMob
deck.blurb: Broadest platform support and the lowest barrier to entry, with a direct pipe to Google's own Search and Display demand no independent SDK can reach. Open Bidding plus waterfall.
deck.risk: Google's own demand competes in the auction it operates, and third-party samples don't show it top by top-grossing-game share.

sdks.name: Digital Turbine (DT Exchange / FairBid)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Not really a mediation play — SingleTap is a patented, one-tap install technology built on deep OEM/carrier device-level integrations, a multi-year relationship moat almost impossible to replicate.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Small-partner concentration risk; comparing its 'market share' to mediation platforms isn't apples-to-apples — it's a different category entirely.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded video; native format limited/forthcoming per vendor docs
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid SDK bidding (OpenRTB) and waterfall via FairBid/DT Exchange SDK — but the real technology sits one layer below, in SingleTap device-level installs.
sdks.reporting: Dynamic Floor Pricing, User Signals API, Impression-Level Data
sdks.privacy: GDPR, IAB Global Privacy Platform (GPP); frequent regional-law updates
sdks.positioning: Publishers seeking OEM/carrier-level distribution alongside monetization
sdks.demandNetwork: Aggregates demand through FairBid/DT Exchange; also integrates into AppLovin MAX, Unity, and Chartboost
sdks.proprietaryTech: SingleTap: one-tap install without app-store redirect (vendor-reported up to +200% conversion lift); Ignite Graph / DT iQ data engines
sdks.marketShare: 1B+ devices, 80,000+ apps reached via on-device integrations

deck.name: Digital Turbine
deck.blurb: SingleTap is a patented one-tap install built on deep OEM and carrier integrations — vendor-reported up to +200% conversion lift, reaching 1B+ devices and 80,000+ apps. A multi-year relationship moat, not an auction product.
deck.risk: Small-partner concentration risk, and its reach is not comparable to a mediation platform's share.

sdks.name: Chartboost Mediation
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Smallest SDK footprint in the category (<340KB) with a no-demand-fee pricing stance; since LoopMe's 2024 acquisition, now the supply-side entry point for 'Chartboost Direct'.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Chartboost Direct is very new (April 2026); actual liquidity/adoption at scale isn't yet established in public sources.
sdks.adFormats: Banner (incl. adaptive), Interstitial, Rewarded, Rewarded Interstitial, Native
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid: OpenRTB 2.5 first-price bidding auction plus waterfall.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android, Unity; also reachable as a mediated network inside AdMob, MAX, and other platforms
sdks.sdkSize: <340 KB combined for iOS, Android, and Unity plug-in
sdks.reporting: Analytics dashboard, bid-distribution-by-winning-bid data, Mediation Reporting API
sdks.privacy: GDPR/US-state consent passed via SDK methods (e.g. addDataUseConsent())
sdks.positioning: Indie and mid-size mobile game studios wanting a lightweight, transparent-bidding SDK
sdks.pricing: No demand fees charged to bidding partners; winning bid equals publisher earnings.
sdks.demandNetwork: Bidding + waterfall partners including AppLovin, AdMob/Google Bidding, InMobi, Digital Turbine Exchange, Liftoff Monetize
sdks.proprietaryTech: 'Chartboost Direct' (April 2026): Direct Pay, Direct Deals, Marketplace Deals — brand-agency programmatic demand on the existing SDK
sdks.marketShare: Mid-tier player relative to AppLovin/Unity; strategically important as LoopMe's mobile supply entry point since 2024

deck.name: Chartboost
deck.blurb: Smallest footprint in the category at under 340KB across iOS, Android and Unity, with a no-demand-fee stance — the winning bid equals publisher earnings. Since LoopMe's 2024 acquisition it is the supply-side entry point for Chartboost Direct.
deck.risk: Chartboost Direct launched April 2026; actual liquidity and adoption at scale are not yet established in public sources.

sdks.name: Vungle (Liftoff Monetize)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Genuinely lightweight SDK (<1MB Android) architected as the exclusive supply-side data source for Liftoff's Cortex DSP.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Same structural conflict as AppLovin/Unity: the SDK's edge comes substantially from feeding the DSP (Liftoff) that also owns it.
sdks.adFormats: App Open, Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, Rewarded Interstitial, Native
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android, Windows, Amazon Fire OS; Unity via mediation adapters
sdks.sdkSize: <1 MB added on Android; ~5.12 MB added on iOS
sdks.privacy: GDPR consent handling built into SDK; ATT/COPPA-specific tooling not detailed — flagged unclear
sdks.positioning: Gaming-heavy publishers; positioned as the lightweight monetization layer feeding Liftoff's UA business
sdks.demandNetwork: Compatible with 'all major mediation platforms'; feeds Liftoff's own Cortex UA engine with exclusive supply signals
sdks.proprietaryTech: Liftoff Exclusive Ads (LXA); the Vungle Exchange gives Liftoff's DSP a claimed ~80% access to unique impressions on that exchange
sdks.marketShare: Company states SDK integrated in '95% of top gaming apps'; per 2026 IPO S-1, combined SDK reaches 160,000+ apps and ~1.4B DAU
sdks.sources: Liftoff Vungle SDK page; Vungle/Liftoff Help Center; BusinessWire; Liftoff 2026 S-1

deck.name: Vungle
deck.blurb: Genuinely lightweight — under 1MB added on Android, ~5.12MB on iOS — and architected as the exclusive supply-side data source for Liftoff's Cortex DSP. Company claims integration in 95% of top gaming apps.
deck.risk: Belongs to Tier 1 economically: the SDK's edge comes substantially from feeding the DSP that also owns it.

sdks.name: MobileFuse
sdks.coreDifferentiator: A demand-side SDK bidder that plugs into other platforms' mediation stacks rather than a standalone mediation platform; duoBid lets video demand fill static banner slots.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Because it's a demand-side plug-in rather than a publisher-adopted mediator, independent market-share data was not found.
sdks.integrationModel: Token-based OpenRTB SDK bidding that plugs into other platforms' mediation; also a Prebid Mobile header-bidding adapter.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android; also via Prebid Mobile header-bidding adapter
sdks.reporting: Not detailed in sources reviewed — flagged unclear
sdks.privacy: Token generation respects opt-out flags; PII (if used) end-to-end encrypted between SDK and exchange
sdks.positioning: Advertisers/demand partners seeking premium in-app, CTV, and DOOH inventory access
sdks.demandNetwork: Functions as a demand source integrated into other platforms' mediation stacks
sdks.proprietaryTech: duoBid: lets video ad demand fill previously static banner inventory (vendor-claimed 20%+ eCPM lift)
sdks.marketShare: Self-describes as 'one of the largest' in-app/CTV/DOOH platforms; independent data not found
sdks.sources: MobileFuse Docs; PR Newswire; Prebid Docs

deck.name: MobileFuse
deck.blurb: A demand-side bidder that plugs into other platforms' mediation. duoBid lets video demand fill previously static banner inventory, with a vendor-claimed 20%+ eCPM lift. Also available as a Prebid Mobile adapter.
deck.risk: A demand-side plug-in rather than a publisher-adopted mediator, so independent market-share data was not found.

openStack.note: Ships a Prebid Mobile header-bidding adapter alongside its own token-based SDK bidding.

sdks.name: CloudX
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Runs its auction inside a Trusted Execution Environment (AWS Nitro Enclave) and has open-sourced the core auction logic itself, so buyers can cryptographically verify the deployed code isn't self-preferencing.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Founded 2025; framed as a 'spiritual successor to MoPub', but actual publisher-adoption scale beyond launch partners is not yet established.
sdks.adFormats: Not explicitly enumerated in vendor materials reviewed — flagged unclear
sdks.integrationModel: Real-time bidding inside a TEE-secured, transparent unified auction; opened to non-SDK omnichannel DSP demand (Jan 2026) without publisher SDK changes.
sdks.platforms: Native Android (Kotlin/Java), Native iOS (Swift/Objective-C), React Native
sdks.reporting: Real-time analytics, log-level access, dynamic price floors, 'CloudX Agent' AI diagnostics
sdks.privacy: Built-in support for GDPR, CCPA, IAB TCF 2.0, GPP, and US Privacy strings
sdks.positioning: Publishers wanting AI-automated, transparent monetization infrastructure — founded by the creators of MoPub and MAX
sdks.pricing: Unified take rate: SDK-based bidders and non-SDK omnichannel DSP buyers pay the same rate.
sdks.demandNetwork: Launch partners: Meta, Liftoff, Magnite; later expanded to Unity, InMobi, Mintegral, Moloco
sdks.proprietaryTech: TEE (AWS Nitro Enclave)-secured, open-sourced core auction logic (github.com/cloudx-io/openauction) with remote attestation
sdks.marketShare: GA reached early 2026; adoption scale beyond launch partners not yet established
sdks.sources: GitHub cloudx-io/openauction; ppc.land; AdExchanger; PR Newswire; TickerTrends

deck.name: CloudX
deck.blurb: Runs its auction inside a trusted execution environment (AWS Nitro Enclave) and has open-sourced the core auction logic, so buyers can cryptographically verify the deployed code isn't self-preferencing. One unified take rate for every buyer.
deck.risk: Framed as a spiritual successor to MoPub, but GA only came in early 2026 — publisher adoption beyond launch partners is not yet established.

openStack.note: Open-sourced the auction core itself (github.com/cloudx-io/openauction) rather than the SDK wrapper — a different and stronger claim.

sdks.name: InMobi
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Geographic depth in Asia-Pacific and emerging markets, plus its own advertiser DSP — but functions mostly as a demand source plugged into AdMob, MAX, and LevelPlay.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Mostly a demand-side role in others' mediation; independent global market-share figures were not found.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, Interstitial, Native, Rewarded video, playables
sdks.integrationModel: Hybrid waterfall/RTB; largely a demand source plugged into AdMob, MAX, and LevelPlay mediation, plus its own publisher SDK.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android (native SDK); reachable via adapters in Unity, Flutter, other mediators
sdks.reporting: A/B testing, price floors, yield-optimization tooling
sdks.privacy: In-house Consent Management Platform (CMP); GDPR, CCPA, TCF, GPP support
sdks.positioning: Publishers/advertisers with strong exposure to Asia-Pacific and emerging markets
sdks.demandNetwork: Plugs into AdMob, MAX, and LevelPlay as a bidding/waterfall demand source; also its own advertiser DSP
sdks.proprietaryTech: In-house CMP; own DSP with multivariate creative testing and format-level bid adjustments
sdks.marketShare: Established player (founded 2007) with recognized geographic strength
sdks.sources: Google Developers InMobi guides; Watsspace; Applixir

deck.name: InMobi
deck.blurb: Geographic depth in Asia-Pacific and emerging markets plus its own DSP and in-house CMP — but functions mostly as a demand source plugged into AdMob, MAX and LevelPlay rather than as a mediator.
deck.risk: Mostly a demand-side role in others' mediation; independent global market-share figures were not found.

sdks.name: Amazon (Publisher Services: TAM/UAM)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Exclusive access to Amazon's own advertiser demand pool via server-side header bidding.
sdks.structuralWeakness: In-app mobile footprint is smaller and far less documented than Amazon's web/header-bidding business.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, pre-roll/rewarded video — delivered via a lightweight APS SDK layered on partner ad-network SDKs
sdks.integrationModel: Server-side header bidding: TAM requires publisher's own demand contracts; UAM is Amazon-managed demand with a disclosed transaction fee.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android via the APS SDK
sdks.reporting: Auction-level reporting showing each bidder's CPM and the winner
sdks.privacy: Relies on partner-network SDKs for GDPR/CCPA consent signaling
sdks.positioning: Larger publishers who already run header bidding and want incremental, Amazon-exclusive demand
sdks.pricing: TAM: small per-CPM fee to bidders. UAM: ~10% transaction fee deducted from SSP bids per a single third-party source — treat as approximate.
sdks.demandNetwork: Amazon's own materials cite '50+ buyers' in one place, 'over 20' in another
sdks.proprietaryTech: Exclusive access to Amazon's own advertiser demand pool
sdks.marketShare: Long-established on web/header-bidding side; in-app mobile footprint smaller/more niche

deck.name: Amazon (TAM / UAM)
deck.blurb: Server-side header bidding with exclusive access to Amazon's own advertiser demand. TAM needs the publisher's own demand contracts; UAM is Amazon-managed with a disclosed transaction fee. In-app footprint is far smaller than the web business.
deck.risk: In-app mobile presence is smaller and far less documented than the web/header-bidding business.

sdks.name: LoopMe
sdks.coreDifferentiator: A 'brand performance' DSP specialist bridging web-native brand/agency budgets into mobile app inventory, operationalized through the Chartboost SDK it has owned since 2024.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Mobile-app relevance is entirely downstream of Chartboost's technical capabilities and adoption.
sdks.adFormats: Pre-roll, vertical video, native, 360, rich-media (DSP-side formats); reaches in-app inventory via the Chartboost SDK
sdks.integrationModel: Primarily a DSP with proprietary 'Intelligent Marketplace' auction; mobile supply access via Chartboost SDK plus 'Chartboost Direct' deal structures.
sdks.platforms: Reaches iOS/Android/Unity apps via the Chartboost SDK rather than its own publisher SDK
sdks.privacy: Not detailed independently; presumed to inherit Chartboost SDK consent handling — flagged unclear
sdks.positioning: Brand agencies and DSPs seeking premium, brand-safe mobile app inventory
sdks.pricing: Revenue via media-transaction take rates plus SaaS-style measurement/data revenue; exact rates not disclosed
sdks.demandNetwork: Launch/marketplace partners not fully enumerated; supply access via Chartboost's mediation partner list
sdks.proprietaryTech: Patented 'Intelligent Marketplace' (6 issued patents, 12 pending) with AI-based ad-request filtering claimed to reduce processing overhead by 98%
sdks.marketShare: Named 'best overall media owner' in the IPA Digital Media Owner Spring 2026 Survey (industry award, not market share)
sdks.sources: LoopMe Intelligent Marketplace page; ppc.land; Adweek; LoopMe News & Blog

deck.name: LoopMe
deck.blurb: A brand-performance DSP bridging web-native brand and agency budgets into app inventory, operationalised through the Chartboost SDK it has owned since 2024. Patented Intelligent Marketplace: 6 issued patents, 12 pending.
deck.risk: Mobile-app relevance is entirely downstream of Chartboost's technical capabilities and adoption.

sdks.name: Liftoff (Accelerate/Direct, DSP)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Unified DSP+SSP architecture built around Cortex, a proprietary neural-network prediction/bidding engine with direct training signal from the Vungle SSP it also owns.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Same structural conflict as the Vungle side: Cortex's edge comes substantially from owning the SSP it buys through.
sdks.adFormats: Rewarded, playable, interstitial, native video (advertiser-side formats)
sdks.integrationModel: Unified DSP+SSP; Cortex-powered DSP buys largely through the Vungle Exchange/Liftoff Monetize supply it also owns.
sdks.platforms: Supply-side footprint = the Vungle SDK; no separate publisher SDK for advertisers
sdks.sdkSize: Shares the Vungle SDK footprint (<1MB Android / ~5.12MB iOS)
sdks.privacy: Inherits Vungle SDK consent handling on the supply side
sdks.positioning: Performance-driven app marketers (gaming, fintech, entertainment, subscription apps) optimizing for ROAS/LTV
sdks.pricing: Outcome-based advertiser pricing (CPI/CPA/ROAS); not a publisher revenue-share model
sdks.demandNetwork: Per 2026 Nasdaq S-1 filings, shared SDK integrated in 160,000+ apps, ~1.4B DAU, 881 demand-side customers in 2025
sdks.proprietaryTech: Cortex: proprietary neural-network prediction/bidding engine, plus vertical-specific 'Adapters'
sdks.marketShare: Filed for Nasdaq IPO (S-1) Jan/Apr 2026; names Google, Meta, Amazon, AppLovin, Unity, and Moloco as key competitors
sdks.sources: Liftoff Accelerate product page; TradingView S-1 coverage

deck.name: Liftoff + Vungle
deck.blurb: Unified DSP+SSP around Cortex, a neural prediction engine trained on the Vungle exchange it owns. Per the 2026 S-1: 160,000+ apps, ~1.4B DAU, 881 demand-side customers.
deck.risk: Cortex's edge comes substantially from owning the SSP it buys through — the same conflict, with an IPO filing now attached.

sdks.name: PubMatic (OpenWrap SDK)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: A Prebid-based open in-app header-bidding wrapper from a public SSP — under 500KB, auctions resolved in under 200ms, and 200+ demand partners reached through direct buyer relationships rather than a network waterfall.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Sells against the mediation incumbents while still needing to sit inside their stacks; the Google Ad Manager adapter remains labelled Beta, and in-app is a minority of PubMatic's overall revenue.
sdks.adFormats: App Open, Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, Rewarded Interstitial, Native
sdks.integrationModel: Prebid-based client-side header bidding via the OpenWrap SDK, plus server-side 'parallel bidding' wrappers; also available as a bidding/waterfall adapter inside Google Ad Manager mediation.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android; adapters for Google Ad Manager and other mediation platforms
sdks.reporting: PubMatic platform analytics with log-level auction data
sdks.privacy: GDPR, CCPA, IAB TCF and GPP support inherited from PubMatic's SSP compliance stack
sdks.positioning: App publishers who want header-bidding mechanics and brand budgets rather than CPI-led network waterfalls
sdks.pricing: No publisher take rate published; PubMatic monetises as an SSP on the media transaction
sdks.demandNetwork: 200+ demand partners including major exchanges and DSPs, with direct buyer relationships positioned for brand spend
sdks.proprietaryTech: OpenWrap SDK (Prebid-based, sub-200ms auction) and a server-side parallel-bidding wrapper
sdks.marketShare: Established public SSP; the in-app SDK is a growing line rather than the bulk of revenue
sdks.sources: PubMatic OpenWrap product pages and case studies; Google Ad Manager mediation docs; PubMatic parallel-bidding blog

deck.name: PubMatic
deck.blurb: A Prebid-based in-app header-bidding wrapper from a public SSP. Under 500KB, auctions in under 200ms, 200+ demand partners, and direct buyer relationships aimed at brand budgets rather than CPI campaigns.
deck.risk: Sells against the mediation incumbents while needing to sit inside their stacks; the Ad Manager adapter is still Beta and in-app is a minority of revenue.

openStack.note: OpenWrap SDK is built on Prebid; PubMatic's Demand Manager Mobile is a Prebid-SDK product. Prebid Mobile itself is open source under Prebid.org.

sdks.name: Ogury
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Fully ID-less brand advertising via 'Personified Advertising' — targets aggregated personas from first-party and contextual signals instead of device identifiers, sold into manually vetted premium app inventory.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Premium CPMs and manual inventory vetting cap scale, and the proposition is brand-first — performance buyers optimising to ROAS are not the target, which narrows the addressable budget.
sdks.adFormats: Interstitial, opt-in and rewarded video, Banner, Thumbnail Ad; vertical and interactive video
sdks.integrationModel: Proprietary publisher SDK plus header-bidding integrations; also available as an SDK bidder inside AppLovin MAX (all formats except Thumbnail) and via Google Ad Manager, Xandr and ironSource adapters.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android; adapters for AppLovin MAX, Google Ad Manager, Xandr, ironSource/Unity
sdks.reporting: Ogury One — persona planning, multi-format campaign setup and real-time performance monitoring
sdks.privacy: ID-less by design; signal-based first-party and contextual targeting, positioned as privacy-first ahead of regulation
sdks.positioning: Brand advertisers and premium app publishers wanting brand budgets without device identifiers
sdks.pricing: Not publicly disclosed; monetises on the media transaction at CPM premiums over open exchange
sdks.demandNetwork: Direct brand and agency demand, plus header-bidding and mediation integrations into the major stacks
sdks.proprietaryTech: Personified Advertising (persona-level ID-less targeting); the Ogury One planning platform
sdks.marketShare: ~$170M revenue (2025, per Rise Session 1 research); 10,000+ manually vetted premium apps
sdks.sources: Ogury publisher help centre and SDK docs; Ogury One product pages; Rise Session 1 research memo (June 2026)

deck.name: Ogury
deck.blurb: Fully ID-less brand advertising. 'Personified Advertising' targets aggregated personas from first-party and contextual signals instead of device IDs, sold into 10,000+ manually vetted premium apps.
deck.risk: Premium CPMs and manual vetting cap scale, and it is brand-first — performance buyers optimising to ROAS are not the target.

sdks.name: Magnite
sdks.coreDifferentiator: The largest independent sell-side company, and as of 2025–26 one of the few with a dedicated in-app SDK built specifically to carry premium brand demand into mobile apps with omnichannel measurement.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Mobile in-app is a late addition to a business built on CTV and web; the SDK is new and its publisher footprint is far smaller than Magnite's overall scale would suggest.
sdks.adFormats: Brand-safe display and video formats via the in-app SDK; full omnichannel format support across the wider platform
sdks.integrationModel: In-app SDK giving direct access to prioritised premium demand, alongside Magnite's exchange, DV+ and private-marketplace deal infrastructure.
sdks.sdkSize: Not publicly disclosed — described only as 'lightweight'
sdks.reporting: Transparency into how ads are served and monetised; omnichannel measurement across the Magnite platform
sdks.privacy: Supports privacy and compliance requirements across regions, inheriting Magnite's SSP compliance stack
sdks.positioning: Premium app publishers wanting brand budgets and PMP deals rather than performance network demand
sdks.demandNetwork: Magnite brand and agency demand via DV+ and private marketplaces; a February 2026 New York Times Advertising collaboration made DV+ its preferred PMP platform for in-app supply
sdks.proprietaryTech: A dedicated in-app SDK for brand-safe mobile formats; DV+ and omnichannel measurement
sdks.marketShare: World's largest independent sell-side company; the in-app SDK footprint is new and not separately disclosed
sdks.sources: Magnite in-app SDK help centre and blog; Unity x Magnite Q&A; Barchart coverage of the NYT Advertising collaboration (Feb 2026)

deck.name: Magnite
deck.blurb: The largest independent sell-side company, now with a dedicated in-app SDK built to carry premium brand demand into apps. NYT Advertising made its DV+ the preferred PMP platform for in-app supply in Feb 2026.
deck.risk: In-app is a late addition to a CTV and web business; the SDK is new and its publisher footprint is far smaller than Magnite's overall scale.

sdks.name: Verve (PubNative / HyBid)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: Ranked North America’s top mobile SSP on both app stores by Pixalate, running an open-source SDK (HyBid 3.0) that connects 150+ brand and performance DSPs on any bidding or mediation platform. Also owns Smaato, so the group position is larger than the Verve brand alone suggests.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Scale is assembled from acquisitions — PubNative, Smaato, and AppMonet’s SDK header-bidding business — rather than one architecture, and open-sourcing the SDK invites the same commoditisation it exploits.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, interstitial, rewarded, native and video across mobile and CTV
sdks.integrationModel: HyBid SDK 3.0 — open-source and modular, works on any bidding or mediation platform — plus the PubNative in-app marketplace and SSP.
sdks.platforms: iOS, Android, CTV; source published on GitHub
sdks.sdkSize: Not publicly disclosed; modular, so publishers include only the components they use
sdks.reporting: Publisher reporting via the Verve/PubNative platform, with SDK data and security practices inspectable through open source
sdks.privacy: Privacy-centric by design: complies with regional and OEM-enforced rules, supports iOS SKAdNetwork and privacy manifests, and is a beta partner for Android Privacy Sandbox
sdks.positioning: Mobile and CTV publishers wanting an open, inspectable SDK carrying both brand and performance DSP demand
sdks.demandNetwork: 150+ brand and performance DSPs; the PubNative marketplace reported 256% revenue growth on Amazon Publisher Services over 18 months (vendor-stated)
sdks.proprietaryTech: HyBid SDK 3.0, open-sourced on GitHub; the PubNative in-app marketplace
sdks.marketShare: Pixalate SSP Market Share Report ranks Verve North America's top mobile SSP on both the Apple App Store and Google Play, held for multiple consecutive quarters
sdks.sources: Verve HyBid SDK 3.0 announcement and integration centre; Verve press releases on the AppMonet and Smaato acquisitions; Pixalate SSP Market Share Report

deck.name: Verve
deck.blurb: North America's top mobile SSP on both app stores per Pixalate, running HyBid 3.0 — an open-source, modular SDK connecting 150+ brand and performance DSPs on any bidding or mediation platform.
deck.risk: Scale is assembled from acquisitions — PubNative, Smaato, AppMonet — rather than one architecture, and open-sourcing the SDK invites the commoditisation it exploits.

openStack.note: HyBid 3.0 is open-sourced on GitHub, and PubNative is documented as a Prebid Mobile bidder.

sdks.name: Moloco
sdks.coreDifferentiator: A machine-learning DSP that has added its own publisher SDK, so the CARA model now trains on supply it owns as well as the demand it buys — the flywheel architecture, assembled by an independent with no mediation platform of its own.
sdks.structuralWeakness: The same structural conflict as AppLovin and Liftoff is now forming here: a DSP that also owns supply. Publisher adoption of roughly 500 apps is an order of magnitude below the mediation incumbents.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, interstitial, rewarded and native; publishers retain creative rendering control
sdks.integrationModel: Publisher SDK letting advertisers bid directly on inventory, certified as a bidding partner inside AppLovin MAX, Unity LevelPlay, Google AdMob and Ad Manager SDK bidding, and across the Nimbus publisher base.
sdks.reporting: Moloco platform reporting with ARPDAU and auction-level performance data
sdks.privacy: Operates on first-party data signals; consent handled through the host mediation platform
sdks.positioning: App publishers wanting direct performance-advertiser demand in the auction, and advertisers buying on first-party data
sdks.pricing: No margin fees — Moloco states cost savings are passed directly to ecosystem partners
sdks.demandNetwork: Moloco's global direct advertiser demand; a certified bidder across MAX, LevelPlay, AdMob, Ad Manager and Nimbus
sdks.proprietaryTech: CARA (Compound Ad Recommendation Architecture) — deep neural networks making billions of bidding decisions daily
sdks.marketShare: Passed a $1B annual revenue run-rate in early 2026 and holds leading independent-DSP share in gaming and commerce; fastest-growing ad network of 2025 by net new SDK integrations (AppGoblin), with roughly 500 publishers
sdks.sources: Moloco SDK product pages and press releases; BusinessWire (July 2025) on AdMob/Ad Manager availability; Nimbus partner page; AppGoblin 2025 report

deck.name: Moloco
deck.blurb: An ML-first DSP that added its own publisher SDK, so CARA now trains on supply it owns as well as demand it buys. Passed a $1B revenue run-rate in early 2026; fastest-growing ad network of 2025 by new SDK integrations.
deck.risk: The same conflict as AppLovin and Liftoff is forming here, and ~500 publishers is an order of magnitude below the mediation incumbents.

sdks.name: Mintegral (Mobvista)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: One of the most widely installed demand adapters in the category — present in roughly 18% of App Store apps using mediation — with particular depth in Chinese-origin gaming demand through parent Mobvista.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Functions as a demand source inside other platforms' auctions rather than as a mediator, so it controls neither the publisher relationship nor the auction, and discloses little about fees or footprint.
sdks.adFormats: App Open, Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, Rewarded Interstitial, Native
sdks.integrationModel: SDK bidding and waterfall adapters inside AppLovin MAX, Google AdMob and Ad Manager, Unity LevelPlay and others; bidding across all formats from adapter 16.5.91.1 onwards.
sdks.reporting: Mintegral publisher platform reporting; secure signals support within Google mediation
sdks.privacy: Consent passed through the host mediation platform; GDPR and CCPA handling via adapter configuration
sdks.positioning: Publishers and advertisers wanting access to global and Chinese-origin gaming demand
sdks.demandNetwork: Mintegral's global advertiser demand via Mobvista, integrated with 10,000+ publishers including Voodoo, Azur Games and CrazyLabs
sdks.proprietaryTech: Mobvista's targeting and creative-optimisation stack behind the Mintegral network
sdks.marketShare: Mediation adapter present in ~17.7% of App Store apps using ad mediation (~49% of downloads) and ~5.7% on Google Play (~21% of downloads), per 42matters
sdks.sources: Google AdMob and Ad Manager Mintegral mediation docs; 42matters SDK analysis; BusinessWire

deck.name: Mintegral
deck.blurb: One of the most widely installed demand adapters in the category — in ~17.7% of App Store apps using mediation, ~49% of downloads — with depth in Chinese-origin gaming demand via parent Mobvista.
deck.risk: A demand source inside others' auctions rather than a mediator, so it controls neither the publisher relationship nor the auction, and discloses little.

sdks.name: Smaato (Verve Group)
sdks.coreDifferentiator: A single-point integration combining an RTB exchange (SMX) with a publisher-side mediation layer. Owned by Verve Group since 2021, so its scale is not independent of Verve’s — the two are one corporate position, not two.
sdks.structuralWeakness: Sits between the larger SSPs and the mediation platforms without a clear technical moat, and since the Verve acquisition its strategic direction and product investment are not separately disclosed.
sdks.adFormats: Banner, video, native, rich media, rewarded
sdks.integrationModel: Publisher SDK with all-in-one mediation and bidding — header-bidding capability plus custom waterfall tiers and priorities, through one integration into the SMX exchange.
sdks.reporting: Publisher platform reporting; dynamic demand ad server
sdks.privacy: GDPR and CCPA support with standard IAB consent framework handling
sdks.positioning: Publishers wanting one integration covering both exchange demand and a mediation layer
sdks.demandNetwork: Smaato Exchange (SMX) — vendor-stated reach of ~450 million unique users across 130 countries, serving 90+ billion impressions per month
sdks.proprietaryTech: SMX exchange with an integrated SSP and mediation layer behind a single integration
sdks.marketShare: Mid-tier global SSP. Acquired by Verve Group (Media and Games Invest) in July 2021 at a $170M enterprise value; no independent post-acquisition share figure found.
sdks.sources: Smaato SDK integration centre; Verve Group / MGI acquisition announcement (July 2021); ExchangeWire and AdExchanger coverage; Publift and MonetizeMore comparisons

deck.name: Smaato
deck.blurb: An RTB exchange (SMX) plus a publisher-side mediation layer in one integration, with vendor-stated 90B+ monthly impressions. Verve has owned it since 2021, so read its scale as part of Verve’s rather than additional to it.
deck.risk: No clear technical moat between the larger SSPs and the mediation platforms, and post-acquisition direction is not separately disclosed.

valueThemes.title: AI yield / data-flywheel optimization
valueThemes.note: Real eCPM lift for publishers, but the model is trained on the same mediator's own DSP traffic — a genuine moat and the source of the self-preferencing critique.

valueThemes.title: Verifiable, non-conflicted auction trust
valueThemes.note: Open-sourced auction core running inside a TEE (AWS Nitro Enclave) — a cryptographic guarantee instead of a policy promise. Currently the only entrant solving this directly.

valueThemes.title: Brand & omnichannel demand access
valueThemes.who: Chartboost Direct (LoopMe), CloudX (omnichannel DSPs), Amazon TAM/UAM
valueThemes.note: Three separate, very recent (2025–2026) attempts to route brand-agency and non-SDK programmatic budgets into mobile app inventory. Real, but early and unproven at scale.

valueThemes.title: Distribution & install-friction removal
valueThemes.note: Solves a completely different problem — one-tap installs via OEM/carrier device integration — not mediation yield. A category of one.

valueThemes.title: Exclusive or differentiated demand pools
valueThemes.who: Amazon (own advertiser demand), InMobi (APAC/emerging-market depth), LoopMe (brand-agency marketplace)
valueThemes.note: Value comes from WHO they can reach, not how the auction works.

valueThemes.title: Lightweight footprint / low integration cost
valueThemes.who: Chartboost (<340KB), Vungle/Liftoff Monetize (<1MB Android), CloudX (AI-agent automated integration)
valueThemes.note: Only {{disclosed.sdkSize}} of {{total}} vendors publish real footprint numbers or make integration speed a differentiator — most don't disclose this at all.

problems.title: Self-preferencing / conflict of interest in the auction
problems.solvedBy: CloudX (verifiable by design); Magnite, Verve/Smaato and PubMatic are sell-side only, so non-conflicted by structure rather than by proof
problems.note: AppLovin, Unity, Google and Liftoff/Vungle all run their own demand inside the auction they operate, and Moloco is now building the same loop. Structural, not technical — only a non-competing operator can credibly avoid it, and only CloudX lets a buyer verify it.

problems.title: Opaque auction mechanics & fee disclosure
problems.solvedBy: Chartboost (no demand fee to bidders), CloudX (unified take rate + public auction code), Moloco (states no margin fees)
problems.note: Publisher take rates are undisclosed by the vendor itself for {{undisclosed.takeRate}} of the {{total}} SDKs tracked here.

problems.title: Brand & omnichannel demand locked out of in-app inventory
problems.solvedBy: Chartboost Direct, CloudX, Amazon TAM/UAM, Magnite, Ogury, PubMatic — six approaches, none at scale
problems.note: The biggest live opportunity in this market, and now the most crowded: six vendors attacking it from different directions, none yet at meaningful scale in-app.

problems.title: No cross-app deduplicated reach/frequency currency for brand planning
problems.note: No mediation SDK here does cross-publisher identity resolution for advertiser planning purposes. This is the clearest whitespace in the whole category.

problems.title: SDK footprint & integration overhead
problems.solvedBy: Chartboost (<340KB), Vungle/Liftoff Monetize (<1MB Android), CloudX (AI-agent automated setup, ~90% faster claimed)
problems.note: Genuinely solved by a minority of vendors who chose to make it a differentiator.

problems.title: Privacy / consent handling (GDPR, CCPA, ATT, COPPA)
problems.note: Baseline table stakes across the industry now. The remaining differentiation is depth, not existence.

problems.title: Signal loss after ATT / IDFA opt-out
problems.solvedBy: AppLovin (Axon contextual/behavioral fallback), Unity (Vector runtime gameplay data), InMobi (own DSP signal)
problems.note: AI platforms with their own first-party demand can partially compensate; smaller demand-side-only players remain more exposed.

problems.title: Ad fraud / IVT verification built into the SDK itself
problems.solvedBy: Not directly addressed by any of the {{total}} in sources reviewed
problems.note: Fraud/IVT verification is still treated as an external, bolted-on layer rather than a native part of any mediation SDK examined here.

problems.title: App-store install friction / drop-off
problems.note: Solved well, but by exactly one vendor, via a fundamentally different device/OEM-level approach.

notes.text: Dashboard seeded from the full 12-SDK research pass (technical capabilities + differentiation + proprietary tech deep-dive). Two fuller written reports with numbered source citations are available from Claude if you need underlying sourcing for any claim here.

Open thread: the defensible "added value" for a new SSP-built SDK looks like (1) verifiable non-conflicted auction (CloudX is the precedent) and (2) closing the brand-currency gap (native pre-bid verification + cross-app deduplicated reach/frequency + curated deal-ID tier). Neither is fully solved by any of the {{total}} yet.

tiers.title: The AI flywheels
tiers.sub: Each pairs a mediation SDK with its own demand, so every impression trains the model that buys the next one.
tiers.footnote: All four run their own demand inside the auction they operate — the moat and the conflict are the same fact.
tiers.notes: These share one architecture: own the supply, own the demand, train on the loop. That is both the strongest moat in the category and the reason auction self-preferencing stays unsolved.

tiers.title: The challengers
tiers.sub: Attacking the incumbents on the two things the flywheels structurally can't offer: verifiable neutrality and a light footprint.
tiers.footnote: CloudX is the only vendor in the snapshot that answers the self-preferencing problem with a mechanism rather than a policy statement.
tiers.notes: CloudX is the most strategically interesting entrant in the set: the existence proof that verifiable auction neutrality is technically shippable.

adjacent.title: Adjacent plays — not really mediation
adjacent.sub: Vendors routinely benchmarked against mediation platforms that are in fact competing on something else entirely.
adjacent.footnote: Independent market-share data was not found for the demand-side bidders — they are adopted by demand partners, not publishers, so publisher-side share is the wrong yardstick.
adjacent.notes: Classification discipline matters here. Digital Turbine’s reach is not comparable to AppLovin’s mediation share, and the demand-side bidders are not competing for the same buyer at all.

selfPreferencing.title: The mediator is also a bidder
selfPreferencing.sub: Several of the mediation platforms run their own demand inside the auction they operate. It is a governance problem, not an engineering one.
steps: Sets the rules, sees every bid, resolves the tie.
Its own DSP competes against the third-party demand it is meant to serve.
Every impression feeds a model that improves its own buying side.
who: Axon feeds both MAX and AppDiscovery, AppLovin's own DSP.
Vector rebuilds the demand side on engine-level gameplay data.
Google's own Search/Display demand competes in Open Bidding.
Cortex buys largely through the Vungle exchange Liftoff owns.
selfPreferencing.footnote: CloudX is the only tracked vendor that addresses this structurally — open-sourced auction logic running in a trusted execution environment.

disclosure.title: What vendors won't tell you
disclosure.sub: Of the SDKs profiled, how many publish each attribute in their own materials.
disclosure.calloutLead: vendors publish their own publisher take rate.
disclosure.calloutBody: Everything else in circulation — AppLovin's rate, AdMob's widely cited "up to 40%", Amazon's ~10% UAM fee — comes from third-party comparisons, not from the vendor. Treat all of it as approximate.
disclosure.footnote: Counts are derived from the vendor profiles in this snapshot; "disclosed" means stated in the vendor's own documentation or filings.

whitespace.title: Where the whitespace actually is
whitespace.sub: For an SSP-built SDK entering this market, the defensible added value reduces to two things — and neither is fully solved by any vendor tracked here.
pillars: CloudX is the precedent, not the ceiling. Open auction logic plus remote attestation turns neutrality from a claim into something a buyer can check. An operator with no competing demand can make that claim more credibly than CloudX can.

Native pre-bid verification, cross-app deduplicated reach and frequency, and a curated deal-ID tier. No cross-app planning currency is claimed by any vendor here — the clearest whitespace in the category.
whitespace.kicker: Everything else in the category is either already won by an incumbent flywheel, or is a category of one that a new SDK cannot replicate.

method.title: How to read this snapshot
method.sub: Sourcing quality varies by vendor and is flagged field by field in the underlying dashboard.
items: Conversion lifts, eCPM gains and adoption claims quoted here are as reported by the vendor. SingleTap's +200% and duoBid's 20%+ are vendor-claimed.
Take rates for most vendors come from comparison sites, not the vendor. AdMob's "up to 40%" and Amazon's ~10% UAM fee both fall in this bucket.
Market share is not comparable across categories
Digital Turbine's device reach, MobileFuse's demand-side role and AppLovin's mediation share measure three different things.
CloudX ad formats, MobileFuse reporting, Vungle ATT/COPPA tooling and LoopMe consent handling were flagged unclear in the source pass.
method.sources: vendor documentation and help centres (AppLovin, Unity, Google, Chartboost, Liftoff, Digital Turbine, Amazon APS, MobileFuse, LoopMe, CloudX) · Liftoff 2026 S-1 and Unity Q1 2026 investor update · AdExchanger, Adweek, ppc.land, Mobile Dev Memo, Naavik, The Register · github.com/cloudx-io/openauction
method.footnote: Two fuller written reports with numbered source citations sit behind this snapshot and can be pulled for any individual claim.
method.notes: Be explicit about sourcing quality when this deck is shown externally. The unresolved fields are listed so nobody treats a gap as a zero.

problemNotes.solved: Note how narrow “solved” is: footprint by three vendors, install friction by exactly one, and via a completely different mechanism.
problemNotes.partial: Brand and omnichannel demand access is the one to watch — three unrelated vendors attacked the same gap within eighteen months, which usually signals the gap is real.
problemNotes.open: These are the strategic content of the deck. The cross-app reach currency in particular is unclaimed by anyone.

implementation.title: Who implements what
implementation.sub: The plumbing in one slide: an app carries one mediation SDK, and everything else is either an adapter compiled into that app or a server-side bid.
lanes: Drops in ONE mediation SDK, then an adapter for each demand partner that needs app-side code. Maps ad units to placements and ships it.
Cost: every adapter added or upgraded means an app-store release.
Owns the SDK, runs the auction, maintains every adapter and reports the results. AppLovin MAX, AdMob and Unity LevelPlay are this layer.
Leverage: it sets the rules of the auction it also sells into.
Networks, DSPs and SSPs supply either an adapter (code inside the app) or a bid endpoint reached server-side (no app code at all).
Server-side demand costs the publisher nothing to add.
implementation.rule: The whole economics of this market sit in one line: demand that needs an adapter costs the publisher an app release, demand that bids server-side costs them nothing. That is why bidding beat the waterfall, and why wrappers exist.
who: One mediation SDK, nothing else. AdMob or MAX. Added adapters cost more in release overhead than they return.
Mediation SDK plus three to six bidding adapters — enough competition to lift eCPM without an unmanageable release burden.
Mediation SDK plus an SSP wrapper (Prebid or OpenWrap) to reach brand budgets the gaming networks do not carry.
Be an adapter inside others' mediation first. A publisher SDK is a years-long distribution problem; prove the demand is worth carrying before asking anyone to ship a release for you.
implementation.footnote: Simplified: it leaves out server-to-server wrappers, SKAdNetwork postbacks and the ad-serving step after the auction resolves.
implementation.notes: If someone takes one thing from this deck, make it the line in the middle. Adapter demand costs an app release; server-side demand is free to add. Every structural fight in this market follows from that asymmetry.

prebid.title: Prebid and the open-source option
prebid.sub: Prebid Mobile is the IAB-adjacent open-source alternative to a proprietary mediation SDK: {{openStack.prebid}} of the {{total}} vendors tracked here offer a Prebid path, and {{openStack.openSource}} publish source for some part of their stack.
scale: of server-side installs managed by SSPs
pros: No single owner of the auction
Public code governed by Prebid.org, so no participant can quietly prefer its own demand.
Demand partners write to a shared interface instead of each being integrated separately.
Anyone can read what the auction does, and ship their own build rather than wait on a roadmap.
Changing SSP is a config change, not an SDK rip-and-replace, which weakens incumbent lock-in.
cons: Someone still has to run it
It removes the owner, not the work — setup, adapter upkeep and yield tuning fall on the publisher.
The big performance networks reach apps via their own SDKs, so pure Prebid leaves gaming eCPM behind.
Open code is not a verified auction
Source proves what the code says, not what the server ran. Only CloudX closes that, with a TEE.
When fill or latency degrades no single vendor is on the hook — which is what a mediation contract buys.
prebid.footnote: "Prebid path" means the vendor ships or documents a Prebid Mobile integration — not merely that it bids into someone else's Prebid auction.
prebid.notes: The honest read: Prebid solves governance, not operations. It answers who controls the auction, and says nothing about who does the work. That distinction is what a commercial wrapper actually sells.

brandOpportunity.title: Where brand and commerce budgets sit
brandOpportunity.sub: In-app is where the audience is and where performance money already lives. Brand and commerce budgets are larger still, and mostly land somewhere else.
stats: of all global digital ad spend is in-app
global retail and commerce media in 2026
of US retail media goes to Amazon and Walmart
of e-commerce traffic originates on mobile

evidence.title: In-app brand advertising does work — the measurement exists
items: 37,000 players across 16 European countries, nine campaigns: average +31% uplift on "a brand for people like me." Pepsi +26%, Visa +18%.
+19pts ad recall, +16pts brand affinity, +15pts brand recall from native in-game placement.
Mobile norms sit at +7.5pts ad recall and +4.4pts purchase intent; in-game campaigns have been measured above those norms on consideration.
CPM premiums of 25–45% over open exchange at 98% viewability — brand money pays more when the environment is guaranteed.

brandOpportunity.readThrough: The budgets are enormous and the effectiveness evidence is now solid. What is missing is the plumbing brand planners need — cross-app reach and frequency, pre-bid verification, a deal-ID tier. That is open gap #4, and it is the reason this money still flows to walled gardens and retail media rather than the open in-app market.
brandOpportunity.footnote: Figures are from different houses on different definitions and do not reconcile: 2026 in-app estimates range from roughly $230B to $425B depending on whether walled-garden social is counted. Treat the direction as reliable and the absolute as approximate.
brandOpportunity.notes: The point of this slide is the read-through, not the numbers. Brand and commerce money is the largest adjacent pool, the effectiveness case is already made, and the blocker is measurement plumbing rather than persuasion.
